sentences: AFP INFO (UPDATED) If a confidence vote ensues, this would put an end to months of political deadlock in the eurozone's fourth-largest economy, which has held 4 general elections in 4 years AT A GLANCE Spanish lawmakers are set to debate the renewal of Pedro Sanchez as prime minister, aiming to resolve a prolonged political deadlock.

MADRID, Spain (UPDATED) – Spanish lawmakers will on Saturday, January 4, begin debating whether to renew Pedro Sanchez as prime minister and end months of political deadlock in the major European Union country.
Sanchez first became prime minister in 2018 when he removed his conservative predecessor Mariano Rajoy in a confidence vote.
Sanchez's coalition with the far-left party Podemos and support from a Catalan separatist party could facilitate his return to power.
Sanchez’s Socialists have already struck a deal with far-left party Podemos to form a coalition government if he wins a confidence vote in parliament following the debate.
The ERC party is considering its position, with hopes for negotiations regarding Catalonia's independence, despite past tensions.
A key Catalan separatist party now looks set to back Sanchez’s bid to stay on in power.

On December 31, Parliament speaker Meritxell Batet informed party representatives that the investiture debate will take place on January 4 and 5 with an extra session slated for January 7 if needed, the assembly said in a statement.
Sanchez needs an absolute majority of at least 176 lawmakers in the 350-seat parliament to take office in a first vote which is expected to take place on January 5.
If he fails this first vote, a simple majority – more yes votes than no – is needed in a second vote that will be held 48 hours later on January 7.

But the Socialists have also secured the backing of several other smaller formations while Catalan separatist party ERC, which won 13 seats in last month’s polls, has said it is willing to abstain from voting which would be enough to allow Sanchez to win the simple majority he needs in the second investiture vote.

“It is difficult for us to trust the Socialist party and the Spanish state but we believe it is an opportunity for separatism which we want to take advantage of,” ERC spokeswoman Marta Vilalta said Monday.
After April’s general election he failed to get parliament’s backing to form a government because his talks with Podemos to form a coalition broke down, sparking the fresh polls.
